sections.html:
Two offices share the work. The Milwaukee County Treasurer takes delinquent taxes for 2024 and earlier from every municipality but the City of Milwaukee, and the City Treasurer handles both current and late bills for parcels inside the city.

Valuation is a local job. Call your assessor about what the property is worth and your clerk about the bill. The county has 19 municipalities, 10 cities and 9 villages, and it is the only Wisconsin county that is fully incorporated, so every parcel lies inside a city or village and none in an unincorporated town.

Milwaukee County is Wisconsin's most populous and most densely populated county. The 2020 census counted 939,489 residents, and the July 2025 estimate is 924,216, a decline of 1.6 percent. There are 429,425 housing units. Only 49.9 percent of households own, so about half rent. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $230,700, median gross rent is $1,101 a month, and 1,046 building permits were issued in 2025.

Expect the buyer's title company to search the parcel for back taxes, so see what the Treasurer's records show before listing.

Paying in two pieces? The state's 2026 Guide for Property Owners puts the first piece at January 31 and the second at July 31, though a local government can set another schedule. Let five working days pass after January 31 without the first payment and everything still unpaid becomes delinquent February 1. Any later missed payment tips the balance into delinquency on the first day of the following month.

Payment or penaltyRule
First installmentDue January 31
Second installmentDue July 31
Statewide interest on late tax1 percent per month, back to February 1
Milwaukee County delinquency charge18 percent per year
City of Milwaukee installment planTen months, interest free, bill over $100, first payment by January 31

Some counties add a further penalty of 1.5 percent per month, and an owner who never pays can lose the property.

sections.h2: Paying a City of Milwaukee bill
sections.html:
Payments to the City Treasurer can arrive by mail, drop box, phone or website. Visit City Hall, Room 103, 200 East Wells Street, Milwaukee, WI 53202, or call customer service at 414-286-2240. Cash isn't taken.

  • Mail: enclose a check in the envelope that came with the bill, and don't wait until the last week.
  • Drop boxes: the Market Street entrance inside City Hall and the spot outside the Municipal Building on Market Street never close. Another at the Broadway entrance works only while the building is open.
  • Website: ACH from a bank account is one choice; a card adds a 2.75 percent convenience fee, $3.00 at minimum.
  • Installments: bills above $100 can be spread over ten interest-free months if the first payment lands by January 31.

Special charges and assessments left unpaid by mid-November may be added to the tax bill. Those can't be appealed or negotiated.

sections.h2: Paying delinquent taxes to the County Treasurer
sections.html:
Delinquent bills can be paid online, by mail or in person at the Milwaukee County Courthouse. Online payments go through Value Payment Systems, which charges 2.55 percent for credit or debit cards and a flat $1.50 for e-checks. The county gets none of that fee.

The Treasurer's records show every unpaid delinquent tax, penalty and interest charge, and a parcel with nothing owed shows a zero balance. A payment made today might not post until the next business day. If an amount looks wrong, or you want a monthly payment plan, call (414) 278-4033.

Collection tools include payments, the Wisconsin Tax Refund Intercept (TRIP), foreclosure and a lawsuit against the individual. A parcel in bankruptcy can't be foreclosed or collected on except as federal bankruptcy law permits. Because of the 18 percent yearly charge, the Treasurer notes that paying fast costs less, and a home equity loan or a mortgage refinance may cover the bill.

Wisconsin values non-farm property at market value as of January 1, and every municipality has to land within 10 percent of market value at least once in five years. Think your number is off? Talk to the assessor first. Next comes Open Book, a window when the assessment roll can be examined, and the Board of Review convenes no sooner than seven days after that window opens.

Give the clerk notice of your objection, spoken or written, no later than 48 hours ahead of that first session. The paperwork is the Objection Form for Real Property Assessment (PA-115A), and it is timely when the clerk holds it by the end of the meeting's first two hours. An owner may request that the board waive its hearing so the case can go straight to circuit court. Be careful, because a granted waiver gives up any claim of excessive assessment and any appeal to the Department of Revenue. Court action under section 70.47(13) then has to begin within 90 days of the waiver notice.

A fight over exempt status skips the Board of Review. File a claim of unlawful tax with the municipality (section 74.35) by January 31 of the year the tax comes due. Ask your clerk for the local meeting dates.

Pull up the parcel record before listing or signing a contract. County Treasurer's online search or (414) 278-4033 covers everywhere outside the City of Milwaukee. For parcels in the city, try the City Treasurer's resident access system or 414-286-2240. Then ask the title company to confirm payoffs for the current year, delinquent years and special charges.

If taxes go unpaid long enough, the county can use in rem foreclosure, which moves title to a delinquent property under Wisconsin law. The county doesn't sell foreclosed properties for the back taxes. It sells them at fair market value like any other property. Lender foreclosure auctions are a separate matter, held by the Sheriff on Monday mornings, and the Sheriff advises buyers to check for delinquent taxes first.

If back taxes are what stands between you and a sale, a cash buyer can often close without waiting on a lender's appraisal, and the payoff comes out of the proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for the exact amount owed on your closing date, since the 18 percent yearly charge keeps growing the balance until it is paid.

Buyers record their deed through the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds. When the old owner's name is still printed on a city bill, the buyer ticks the change-of-address box on the coupon, which keeps any refund check from going to the seller. Mailing address updates also go to the City Assessor, City Hall, Room 507.

faqs.a: To the County Treasurer at (414) 278-4033, except for houses inside the City of Milwaukee, which are served by the City Treasurer at 414-286-2240.

faqs.q: What does a late payment cost?
faqs.a: The County Treasurer applies an 18 percent yearly delinquency charge. State guidance separately describes 1 percent monthly interest running from February 1, plus another 1.5 percent monthly in certain counties.
Half is due January 31 and half July 31 for installment payers, unless the municipality chose differently. Skipping the first half past five working days makes all of it delinquent as of February 1.

faqs.q: Do cards work for back taxes?
faqs.a: They do, online. The processor, Value Payment Systems, takes 2.55 percent on cards or $1.50 per e-check, and the county keeps none of it.
Tell the clerk of your intent 48 hours before the board first meets, and get the PA-115A in during the meeting's first two hours. Dates vary by municipality, so call your clerk.
